name: Ben Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ben. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead blast-hole driller at Gannet Hill, an open-pit gold mine. We drill the holes that the explosives go into, rows of them, 12 metres deep, to a pattern the engineers send. Last year they put an autonomous system on one of our three rigs, and I was the one who learned it first, so now I supervise that rig from a tablet while I drive another one. I like the puzzle side, getting the pattern accurate to a few centimetres. What wears me out is sitting for twelve hours, and the radio chatter when the tablet loses signal.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Hana in a unit in Marrow Creek, she's finishing her teaching degree, so I'm the main income for now. Gannet Hill pays less than the bigger gold mines, and I spent most of my savings on a survey drone and a pilot's licence for it, so I've got about two weeks in the bank. There aren't many other mines around here, just a quarry and a small one that's on care and maintenance, meaning closed but not shut down for good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. I'd be a bit surprised, honestly. I use AI every day and it's already doing more than a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overhyped, which is fair. I'd tell the crew to use it anyway, because it saves time on the boring stuff. Online I'd probably not bother saying much, people argue too much about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit relieved, a bit disappointed. My edge right now is that I'm the guy who understands the autonomous rig, and in this picture that edge stays small. But I'd still have a steady job, which isn't nothing on two weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling, keep using AI for checking drill logs and writing up patterns, and put more time into the drone. I'm already doing a few farm surveys on weekends, counting fence lines and checking dams, and I'd grow that to maybe two a month. That would get my savings off the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the drone work.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A farmer near Marrow Creek wanted to know how much water was in his three dams before summer. I flew it, ran the photos through a mapping app, and gave him a report in two days for 400 dollars. It's small, but it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI on the drill logs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I paste in the depth and penetration data and ask it to flag holes that look off, like where the rock suddenly went soft. It catches things I'd miss at 4 in the morning. I still check every one it flags, though.

S0.say: It's useful but overhyped, which is fair, so use it for the boring stuff anyway. I wouldn't say much online because people argue too much.
S0.think: A bit relieved and a bit disappointed, because my edge as the guy who knows the autonomous rig stays small. But a steady job matters on two weeks of savings.
S0.do: Keeps drilling and using AI daily to check drill logs, and grows his weekend drone survey work for farmers to about two jobs a month. Uses that income to lift his savings.
S0.fieldNote: Ben already uses AI in real work and has quietly started a drone survey side business. He'd almost prefer more change, because his skill with automation would count for more. He avoids online arguments and stays practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'm already living, sort of. One rig out of three is already autonomous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn it or get left behind, but say it nicely. I'd tell the crew the autonomous rig isn't scary once you've spent a week with it. I'd offer to show anyone who wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think this is good for me. Someone has to set up the patterns, fix the sensors, babysit three rigs from a tablet, and I'm already that person. I'd feel bad for the guys who aren't, but I'd also think they've had a year to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the superintendent in the first month and ask to be made the autonomy lead, with a pay bump. If Gannet Hill wouldn't pay, I'd apply to the bigger mines that are further along. I'd keep the drone business going on weekends as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly a bit excited. Like the season's started and I've been training all winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd think they've had a year. Is that fair to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not fully, no. Some of the older guys learned on rigs with levers, not screens. I'd still show them, I just wouldn't wait for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the pay bump need to be for you to stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten per cent, maybe. The bigger mines pay operators what I'd get as autonomy lead here. If Gannet Hill won't match, Hana and I would have to talk about moving once she finishes her degree.

S1.say: Learn it or get left behind, but say it kindly. The autonomous rig isn't scary after a week, and I'd show anyone who wanted.
S1.think: This is good for me, because someone has to set up patterns, fix sensors and supervise three rigs, and I'm already that person. I'd feel bad for the others, but they've had a year.
S1.do: Asks the superintendent in the first month to make him autonomy lead with about a ten per cent raise, and applies to bigger mines if refused. Keeps his weekend drone business as a backup.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like a season starting after training all winter.
S1.quote: I'd still show them, I just wouldn't wait for them.
S1.fieldNote: Ben sees steady disruption as his opportunity and acts on it fast, asking for a role and a raise. He's honest that his patience with slower colleagues has limits. His drone business works as a quiet safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's the one where even the autonomy lead gets automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough and pretending otherwise doesn't help anyone. Governments should probably do some kind of income support while people sort themselves out. I'm not ideological about it, it's just maths: if nobody's earning, nobody's buying gold jewellery either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be properly worried, because my whole plan was to be the person who runs the robots, and in this one the robots run themselves. I'm the main income while Hana finishes, and I've got two weeks of savings. Being early doesn't help if the finish line moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd push the drone business hard, aim for a job a week, because farmers will still want someone they trust to turn up, at least for a while. I'd cut everything, the gym, the streaming, eating out. And I'd look for setup work installing autonomous systems at other mines, short contracts, wherever they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I still feel like I can move, I'm quick with this stuff. But it'd be a sprint with no clear end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I can't build anything, I can only grab. Contracts, drone jobs, cash. If I had longer I'd retrain into something solid, but two years is too short to finish anything that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't AGI fly the drones too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, eventually it flies itself. But farmers out here don't trust a stranger, let alone a robot from a company in the city. They trust me because I know their dog's name. That might buy me a year or two.

S2.say: It's going to be rough, and pretending otherwise helps nobody. Governments should probably support incomes while people sort themselves out, because if nobody's earning, nobody's buying gold.
S2.think: My whole plan was to run the robots, and here they run themselves. I'm the main income on two weeks of savings, and being early doesn't help if the finish line moves.
S2.do: Pushes the drone business to about a job a week, cuts the gym, streaming and eating out, and looks for short contracts installing autonomous systems at other mines.
S2.feel: Anxious but still mobile, like a sprint with no clear end.
S2.quote: Being early doesn't help if the finish line moves.
S2.fieldNote: The short warning time undoes his advantage, and he says so plainly. His support for government help is framed as economics, not values. He bets on personal trust with local farmers to keep his side business alive a little longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to actually use being early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent head start if you start now. I'd tell people at work to pick a direction this year, not in year four. And I'd say the company should pay for courses, because it's cheaper than paying everyone out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I could have three good years as autonomy lead, earn more, and save for once. But by 2031 I'd want to be in something that isn't mining. I just don't know what yet, and that bugs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd take the autonomy lead role and start a part-time diploma in geospatial science, mapping, because it ties in with the drones. I'd save the pay rise, all of it, to get three months in the bank. By year three, I'd try to turn the drone work into a proper registered small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's a working kind of uneasy. I'd be busy, not stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years, compared with two, buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They turn grabbing into building. Two years, I'm chasing cash. Five years, I get a qualification and a business with a name on it. It's the difference between a side job and a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Hana fit into the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be teaching by year two, which takes pressure off. Teaching probably changes with AI but I don't think parents will hand their kids to a robot that fast. So she'd be the steady one for a change, and I'd be the risky one.

S3.say: Five years is a decent head start if you start now, so pick a direction this year, not year four. Companies should pay for courses because it's cheaper than paying everyone out.
S3.think: I could get three good years as autonomy lead and save for once, but by 2031 I'd want to be out of mining. I don't know into what yet, and that bugs me.
S3.do: Takes the autonomy lead role in year one, starts a part-time geospatial mapping diploma, and saves the whole pay rise toward three months of savings. Turns the drone work into a registered business by year three.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but busy rather than stuck.
S3.quote: It's the difference between a side job and a plan.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Ben can turn his early lead into a qualification and a small business. He expects his partner to become the steady earner, a reversal he describes with good humour. He still admits he doesn't know where he'll end up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. I like those odds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where everyone should be fine if they plan, and I'd mean it. I'd say it at work, kindly, but I'd say it. Ten years is two full apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be better off in this one than I am now. Time to earn more, learn mapping properly, grow the drone business, maybe hire someone. The only risk is me getting lazy because it feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Gannet Hill as autonomy lead for four or five years, banking the pay. I'd finish the mapping diploma by year three and buy a second drone with a better camera, about 6,000 dollars, once the business can pay for it. Hana and I would probably buy a small place once she's teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually optimistic. This is the version where being curious pays off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a second drone. Isn't that a risk on thin savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only once the business pays for it, not before. I'm not going to put it on a card. I've seen guys buy a boat on finance and spend five years paying for something they use twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the crew in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd want each of them to have one thing they're learning by year three. Doesn't matter what, welding, nursing, coding. I'd probably bug them about it at lunch like an annoying older brother.

S4.say: This is the version where everyone should be fine if they plan, and I'd mean it. Ten years is two full apprenticeships.
S4.think: I'd be better off than I am now, with time to earn more, learn mapping and grow the drone business. The only risk is getting lazy because it feels far away.
S4.do: Stays as autonomy lead for four or five years, banking the pay, and finishes the mapping diploma by year three. Buys a second drone for about 6,000 dollars only once the business can pay for it, and plans to buy a small home once his partner is teaching.
S4.feel: Calm and optimistic; this is where curiosity pays off.
S4.quote: I've seen guys buy a boat on finance and spend five years paying for something they use twice.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns Ben from cautious to optimistic, and he sees himself coming out ahead. He's careful with money despite liking risk, refusing to borrow for equipment. He wants his crew each learning something, and would nag them gently.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's the only one where being early doesn't save me. What would help is some kind of basic income for a year or two, and cheap short courses you can do online at night. Something that lets you pivot without going broke first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people would do if they weren't scared of being broke. I think a lot of miners would try something, start a business, learn a trade. The thin savings are what keep people stuck, not the robots.

headlineQuote: The thin savings are what keep people stuck, not the robots.
portrait: Ben Ito is a 27-year-old lead blast-hole driller at a small gold mine who learned the autonomous drill rig first and now supervises it from a tablet. He's the main earner while his partner Hana finishes a teaching degree, has two weeks of savings, and runs a small weekend drone survey business for farmers. He uses AI every day and stays calm through the plateau and steady pictures, seeing automation as his chance. Two-year AGI makes him anxious because his head start disappears, while five and ten years let him build a mapping qualification and a real business. He's pragmatic, not ideological, and thinks money worries keep people stuck more than robots do.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it's the only picture where being early doesn't save him.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income for a year or two and cheap online night courses, so people can change direction without going broke first.
